zone: Mount Baker Highway front — Heather Meadows and Canyon Creek
_areas_note: Two road systems off the Mount Baker Highway east of Glacier, and both are front-country in a way almost nothing else in this catalog is. The first is the paved highway itself above Heather Meadows: Table Mountain rises straight off the Artist Point turnaround at the road end, Mount Herman is climbed from the Bagley Lakes trailhead across from the ski area by way of Herman Saddle and the south ridge, and Mount Ann is a scramble leaving the Lake Ann trail from the Austin Pass trailhead a little below Artist Point. The second is Canyon Creek Road, which leaves the highway about two miles east of Glacier and runs north; Bearpaw Mountain is reached from a short spur off it to Bearpaw Lake, and the same road ends at the Damfino Lakes trailhead. THREE PEAKS WERE REMOVED AFTER CHECKING THEIR REAL APPROACHES. The Pleiades is not on either road: it is climbed from the Twin Lakes road, up the High Pass trail and over a col in the south arm of Mount Larrabee, and its camping is the Twin Lakes basin and the Gargett Mine basin already written in the Twin Lakes file. Mamie Peak is on the Hannegan Pass road (FS 32) — it is the tiered granite wall directly above the Hannegan Pass trailhead, visible a few minutes up the trail — so its camping belongs with the Ruth Creek and Nooksack Cirque peaks, not here. Indian Mountain is not a road-served peak at all: it stands above the Brush Creek valley near Whatcom Pass, deep inside North Cascades National Park roughly seven miles south of the Canadian border, and is reached on foot over Hannegan Pass and down the Chilliwack River — a multi-day trip under a park backcountry permit that shares nothing with a Canyon Creek Road day out. NOT DUPLICATED: the Lake Ann basin camp is already described in the Mount Shuksan file and is the obvious night out for a party on Mount Ann, so it is deliberately absent here; the Twin Lakes basin, Winchester Lookout, High Pass and Gargett Mine sites are in the Twin Lakes file; and the Hannegan and Boundary camps are in the Chilliwack file. THE HONEST FRAMING OF THE HEATHER MEADOWS PEAKS is that they are short day scrambles from a paved road, several of them under two miles from the car, and nobody plans an overnight for them. What follows still covers where you sleep, because a party that runs long, gets weathered, or wants to be on the summit at first light needs somewhere legal to be — and because the high ground here is under some of the strictest camping rules in the district.

sites.name: Artist Point and the Heather Meadows road end
sites.capacity: A large paved turnaround at Artist Point and a second big lot at Heather Meadows below it; parking for many vehicles, and NO legal camping at either. Treat this as a start line rather than a site.
sites.water: None. There is no potable water anywhere along this stretch of road or on the trails above it, and every lake and stream on the Chain Lakes circuit has to be treated.
sites.permit: A recreation pass must be displayed at Artist Point and at the Bagley Lakes trailhead; the state parks pass is not valid at these Forest Service sites. There is a self-issue wilderness register near the trailhead. The camping rules here are the strict part and they are easy to fall foul of: camping is prohibited on Table Mountain from mid-May to mid-November, prohibited at the Bagley Lakes trailhead over the same window, and prohibited within a mile of the Chain Lakes trail junction on the Ptarmigan Ridge side. Camping outside that window, in deep winter, is legal on Table Mountain. Party size in the wilderness is capped at twelve, campfires are prohibited outright and only carry-in stoves are allowed, and dogs must be leashed through the developed area.
sites.notes: This entry exists to say plainly that the obvious place to sleep is the one place you cannot. Table Mountain is a short, steep switchbacked climb from the Artist Point lot and is usually done in an hour or two; Mount Herman goes from the Bagley Lakes trailhead across from the ski area, past the lakes and up towards Herman Saddle, leaving the trail at the last switchback for the ridge between Mazama Dome and the summit; Mount Ann leaves the Lake Ann trail at the Austin Pass trailhead a little below Artist Point and is a much bigger day, around ten and a half miles with four thousand feet of gain, ending in a genuine scramble. All three are car-to-car objectives for a fit party. THE SEASONAL GATE IS THE PLANNING CONSTRAINT: the last stretch of highway above Heather Meadows to Artist Point is narrow, steeply banked and closed to vehicles every winter, typically shutting somewhere between mid-October and the start of November with the first real snow and not reopening until the plows get through, which in a heavy year is well into July. The highway is kept open to Heather Meadows through the winter for the ski area, so a closed gate costs you the top two and a half miles rather than the whole road. Parties arriving before the gate opens are walking or skinning that section with the peaks still under snow, which changes all three from scrambles into snow climbs.

sites.name: Silver Fir Campground
sites.capacity: About twenty sites in forest beside the North Fork Nooksack, with vault toilets and drinking water in season; first come, first served, and it fills on summer weekends
sites.water: Piped water at the campground during the operating season, and the river alongside. Confirm the water is turned on if you are arriving at the shoulders of the season.
sites.permit: A campground fee is charged per night and paid on site; this is a fee campground rather than a pass site, so a recreation pass does not cover the overnight. Fires are allowed in the provided rings unless a county or forest-wide burn ban is in force, which through a dry August is common. Standard national forest food-storage sense applies — black bears work this valley.
sites.notes: The closest developed campground to the Heather Meadows end of the highway, roughly fourteen miles east of Glacier on the west side of the road just after the river crossing, and about eight miles below the Heather Meadows lots. This is the practical answer for a party that drives up the night before a scramble on Table Mountain, Mount Herman or Mount Ann and wants to be at the trailhead early without sleeping in a day-use car park. It is emphatically staging rather than plan: you are three thousand feet below the objectives and the drive up in the morning takes twenty minutes. Because there are no reservations it is a gamble on a Friday evening in July and August, and the fallback is the campground further down the valley. It stays open later into the autumn than the road to Artist Point does, which matters for anyone climbing these peaks in October.

sites.name: Douglas Fir Campground
sites.capacity: Around thirty sites in old growth beside the North Fork Nooksack, with vault toilets and seasonal drinking water; reservable in advance, which is the reason to choose it over the campground higher up
sites.water: Piped water in season plus the river. Treat river water.
sites.permit: Per-night campground fee, bookable ahead through the national reservation system, so unlike the higher campground you can arrive at ten at night and know you have a site. Campfire rings are provided and are subject to seasonal burn bans. A recreation pass does not cover camping here.
sites.notes: Two and a half miles east of Glacier, low in the valley and a long way below anything you would climb — but it is the campground that serves BOTH halves of this zone, because the Canyon Creek Road turning is only a couple of miles back down the highway. A party bound for Bearpaw Mountain has a rough, slow forest road ahead of them in the morning and this is the sensible place to be the night before; a party bound for Heather Meadows has a longer drive up than they would from the higher campground but a guaranteed bed. Being at a thousand feet in dense timber it is warm, damp and mosquito-prone in early summer, and it gives you no acclimatisation and no view. The upside is that it is open when the high country is not, and that it is the only bookable option on this side of the mountain.

sites.name: Mazama Lake designated sites, Chain Lakes
sites.capacity: Four designated sites marked by posts with a tent symbol, and a backcountry toilet. First come, first served, with no reservations and no permit to obtain — which means four parties get in and the fifth has nowhere legal to go.
sites.water: The lakes, and they are reliable all season. There is no potable water anywhere on the circuit, so treat everything.
sites.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, Mount Baker Wilderness. No overnight permit is required or issued. Recreation pass on the vehicle at whichever of the four trailheads you start from. CAMPING IS RESTRICTED TO THE MARKED SITES — the meadows here are heather over thin soil and the designation exists because they were being destroyed. No campfires at all, carry-in stoves only. Party size twelve. Food must go in a bear-resistant canister or be hung at least ten feet up and four feet out from the trunk and branches; there is no hardware provided.
sites.notes: The nearest legal backcountry camping to the Heather Meadows peaks and the only overnight option in the immediate basin, in the string of subalpine lakes that the Chain Lakes trail drops into on the far side of Herman Saddle. From Artist Point the circuit is around six miles with roughly seventeen hundred feet of gain and loss, and the lakes sit a bit under halfway round. For Mount Herman this is genuinely useful: the saddle is on the route, so a party that camps here is above the trailhead with a very short morning to the south ridge. For Table Mountain it is a detour rather than an approach, and the reason to know about it is the ban on camping on Table Mountain itself through the summer. Snow lingers in the basin into mid-August in a heavy year, which is worth knowing before committing to a site that may be under a drift. Trekking poles earn their weight on the snow traverses. This is a busy, family-friendly circuit and the sites go early on a summer weekend, so arrive with a plan for finding all four taken.

sites.name: Hayes Lake designated sites, Chain Lakes
sites.capacity: Four designated sites marked with posts, slightly more open and more exposed than the lower lake, with a pit toilet on the stretch between Iceberg Lake and here
sites.water: The lake, treated. Iceberg Lake nearby holds floating ice well into summer and is the colder and less pleasant draw of the two.
sites.permit: Mount Baker Wilderness, same rules as the sister camp: no overnight permit, recreation pass at the trailhead, camping only at the marked sites, no fires of any kind, party limit twelve, food canistered or hung with no provided hardware. Nothing here is reservable, so the eight sites across both lakes are the entire legal capacity of the basin on any given night.
sites.notes: The upper pair of the Chain Lakes camps, a short distance on from the lower lake and a little higher, closer to the climb back up to Herman Saddle. For a party that has come over from the Artist Point side and intends to finish the circuit in the morning this is the better position, and it catches the evening light on Baker; for a party using the basin as a base for Mount Herman it is marginally further from the saddle than the lower lake and marginally more exposed to weather coming across the ridge. Elevation is not stated because the usable ground spreads across the shore rather than sitting at one identifiable point. Everything the basin holds is heavily used — camp on the marked pads, keep well back from the shoreline, and do not add a ninth site because the eight are taken. The right answer when they are full is to walk out; the trailhead is not far and the road is paved.

sites.name: Bearpaw Lake
sites.capacity: A few rough informal sites at a small lake in the trees; low use, no facilities, no toilet and nothing built
sites.water: The lake, at camp. Treat it. This is the only water on the peak's own approach and there is nothing on the ridge above.
sites.permit: Mt Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest, OUTSIDE any designated wilderness — this ground sits west of the Mount Baker Wilderness boundary, so there is no self-issue permit and no wilderness party limit here, and the twelve-person rule and blanket fire ban that govern the Heather Meadows half of this zone do not automatically apply. What does apply is a recreation pass at the trailhead, and whatever county or forest-wide burn ban is in force, which through a dry summer is usually a total one. Pack out everything including human waste; there is no toilet.
sites.notes: The base for Bearpaw Mountain and the only camping anywhere near its own line. Canyon Creek Road leaves the Mount Baker Highway about two miles east of Glacier and runs north for a long, slow fourteen miles or so of alternating tarmac and serious potholes before a signed spur climbs right to the lake trailhead; the last couple of miles are single lane with brush closing in that will mark a car. From the trailhead it is roughly a mile to the lake, short but steep. The peak's easiest line is a class three scramble from the southwest, following the timbered ridge east of the lake, with a direct variation onto the steeper part of the ridge that gives a narrow and locally exposed scramble. ROAD ACCESS IS THE FIRST THING TO CHECK AND NOT AN AFTERTHOUGHT: Canyon Creek Road has been closed at around mile four by a landslide carrying large timber and debris, with more downed trees below the block, which cuts off the lake spur and the road end entirely. When that closure is in force there is no alternative approach to this peak, only a very long road walk. Snow lies on this ground into July in most years.

sites.name: Excelsior ridge camps and the high spring, Canyon Creek Road end
sites.capacity: Scattered informal sites on the ridge running south from Excelsior Peak and along the High Divide, plus a cluster near the spring; a handful of small parties, spread out, with no built sites and no toilet
sites.water: A spring about half a mile short of Excelsior Pass is the best and most dependable water in this high country and is the reason the camps are where they are. The lakes lower down at the trailhead end are shallow and warm late in the season. Treat everything, and fill at the spring rather than counting on anything on the crest.
sites.permit: The ridge camps sit inside the Mount Baker Wilderness, which the High Divide trail enters at the pass — so from there on it is party size twelve, no campfires of any kind, carry-in stoves only, camp on durable ground and pack out all waste including human waste. A recreation pass is required at the trailhead and there is a self-issue register. The ground below the pass around the lakes is outside the wilderness and less strictly governed, but the burn bans still apply.
sites.notes: This is the established high camping on the Canyon Creek road system, at the far end of the same road that serves Bearpaw, and it is listed with the caveat that IT IS NOT ON BEARPAW'S OWN ROUTE. Bearpaw is the prominent summit standing to the west, seen across the drainage from the pass and the ridge, and reaching it from here means dropping and re-climbing rather than walking a connecting line. Its value is as the answer to what a party does when the day goes wrong or when they want two objectives out of one long, slow drive: legal, watered, established camping at the road end of a road most people will only want to drive once. The trail leaves the road end, meets a junction in less than a mile with the Canyon Ridge trail going left, reaches the small lakes just beyond and then climbs through forest and into open meadow towards the pass. The same landslide closure that gates the Bearpaw spur gates this trailhead as well; the alternative is to walk up from the highway instead, which is a far bigger day. Meadows here are at their best in July and August and again for autumn colour in September and October.
